newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo says Argentine graft worries investors.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo says Argentine graft worries investors.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo said in an interview published Wednesday that long-term investors in Argentina were worried about corruption and court cover-ups, against which he is campaigning.

Speaking in New York to the Argentine newspaper Clarin, the free-market reformer dismissed by President Carlos Menem in July said "people who see Argentina as a place to make short-term gains may only be mildly concerned about this debate."
But he said businesses "who are going to make investments for many years are extremely worried that there is corruption or that the legal system does not work well."

Cavallo, who was widely praised for his economic reforms and for taming inflation, has named senior Menem ministers and judges in his crusade against graft. He goes to court Dec 18 to be tried on charges of slandering a Supreme Court judge.

Cavallo's criticisms have also touched his successor Roque Fernandez, once a central bank chief, whom he called "either incompetent or dishonest" for condoning a businessman Cavallo accuses of heading a drug-linked "mafia".

Despite the possibility of going to jail, the Harvard-trained Cavallo has announced plans to run for Congress next year and eventually for president. He told Clarin he was confident he had the support of the Argentine people.
"I feel accompanied in the best way possible -- by the Argentine people, who are the ones who vote," he said.
The ex-minister said the debate he has opened has been welcomed in the United States: "Here they believe that only countries who discuss their problems can solve them."
Asked about declared candidates for the Peronist ticket to succeed Menem in 1999, Cavallo called former Tucuman governor Ramon Ortega "credible".
But he cautioned that Eduardo Duhalde, the party's second-in-command and Buenos Aires governor, about his ally Alberto Pierri, president of the lower house of Congress.
"He is a man who I think wants to fight corruption. But as long as one of his main supporters is Alberto Pierri, who is going to believe he is going to fight corruption?" Cavallo said.
